verdict.reasoning: Patient states, “over the past few days I’ve noticed my skin is sore and red” and that it is “very itchy,” and later says it is “getting worse, like, the past few days. Way worse.”

Location described as “all over my chest, my hands and arms, and especially inside of the elbows… which is the worst area,” which corresponds to diffuse over chest, hands, arms, worst in antecubital fossae.
Patient says the skin is “very itchy and, uh, dry, all over my body” and clarifies weeping: “No. No. … but, but, not the areas that are cracked,” confirming dryness, cracks, and no weeping.
Doctor asks, “Otherwise, other than those rash, you're feeling well… There's no temperature, no joint pains, yeah? No fever?” and patient does not object, implying no fever or joint pain reported.
Doctor: “you've mentioned you've got a history of eczema,” and the discussion repeatedly refers to her “usual eczema.”
Patient: “I, I have asthma,” and later they discuss her asthma medications.
Patient: “usually I use a a a cream called diprobase.”
Patient: “in the shower I use something called dermal,” and doctor later: “your, emollients like the dermal soap,” consistent with Dermol/dermal wash use.
Doctor: “So you're using the Hydrocortisone, yeah?” Patient: “Yes.” This indicates over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream use.
Doctor: “The blue inhaler? So you don't, you don't use it everyday, so you just use it on and off, yeah?” Patient agrees. Blue inhaler in asthma context implies salbutamol PRN.

Patient: “I remember that I've tried [antihistamines] and it didn't work.” Doctor: “Which one did you try?” Patient: “The one over-the-counter.” Doctor: “OK, so like cetirizine, yeah?” indicating ineffective OTC cetirizine-type antihistamine.
Doctor: “Do you have any allergies to any medication at all?” Patient: “No, no allergies.”
Patient: “in my family, uh, there's hypothyroidism and migraine. My mother has migraine.” Then clarifies mother has hypothyroidism as well. So mother has migraine and hypothyroidism.

Doctor concludes “it looks like… it is quite widespread, your eczema,” and patient reports it is “very itchy and dry,” with “cracks” and “No. No” to weeping, and no systemic symptoms; this supports a widespread, pruritic, dry, cracked, non‑infected atopic dermatitis flare.

Asthma use: “The blue inhaler? So you don't, you don't use it everyday, so you just use it on and off, yeah?” Patient agrees, and “your breathing's all OK, yeah?” “OK, yeah, yeah.” This supports intermittent, currently stable asthma managed with PRN SABA.
Doctor: “we'll, you would probably need some antihistamines, which I'm going to prescribe… it's called the antihistamine is called Fexofenadine.” (oral antihistamine).

Doctor: “You might probably need a bit more stronger one, like betnovate or something like that… we'll try with some Betnovate first… You have to use it twice a day, for the next couple of weeks.” This implies Betnovate cream/ointment thin layer BID for ~2 weeks.
Doctor: “You still need to continue on your, emollients like the dermal soap, and, as well as the, diprovate [Diprobase].”

Doctor: “If, if there's no improvement, you need to get back to us. Or, if you have any kind of adverse reaction… you need to get in touch with us… If things are getting worse in the next two weeks, call us before hand. Otherwise, wait for two weeks.”
Doctor: “we're going to send off the prescription to your pharmacy. It looks like Boots on the systems, is that correct? … so i'll send it across to Boot's. And it will be there for collecting.”

The transcript confirms current PRN blue inhaler use but the doctor does not explicitly state a plan to “continue salbutamol inhaler as needed.” This continuation is implied but not directly documented as part of the plan.
